grammar.prompt: She ___ to work by bus every day.
grammar.explanation: 'Every day' shows a routine → present simple. With he/she/it, add -es: goes.

grammar.prompt: I ___ my keys yesterday, so I couldn't get into my flat.
grammar.explanation: 'Yesterday' is a finished time in the past → past simple (lost). The present perfect is not used with 'yesterday'.

grammar.prompt: This flat is ___ than the one we saw last week.
grammar.explanation: Short adjectives form the comparative with -er + than: big → bigger.

grammar.prompt: There isn't ___ milk in the fridge. Can you buy some?
grammar.explanation: Use 'any' in negative sentences. 'Milk' is uncountable, so not 'many' or 'a'.

grammar.prompt: We ___ in this city since 2019, so we know it very well.
grammar.explanation: An action that started in the past and continues now, with 'since' → present perfect.

grammar.prompt: I ___ a shower when the lights suddenly went out, so I had to finish in the dark.
grammar.explanation: A longer action in progress (was having) is interrupted by a short action (went out) → past continuous.

grammar.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay at home and watch a film.
grammar.explanation: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb. Don't use 'will' after 'if'.

grammar.prompt: If I ___ more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
grammar.explanation: Second conditional (an imaginary present situation): if + past simple, would + verb.

grammar.prompt: Most of the vegetables in this shop ___ by local farmers.
grammar.explanation: The vegetables don't grow themselves here — farmers grow them. Present simple passive: are + past participle.

grammar.prompt: When I was a child, I ___ play football every weekend, but now I never have time.
grammar.explanation: 'Used to + verb' describes a past habit that is no longer true. 'Be used to' means 'be familiar with'.

grammar.prompt: I'm really looking forward to ___ (see) you next week.
grammar.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form.

grammar.prompt: I'm exhausted. I ___ on this report since eight o'clock this morning.
grammar.explanation: An activity that started in the past and is still continuing, with 'since' → present perfect continuous.

grammar.prompt: 'Where do you live?' he asked. → He asked me where ___.
grammar.explanation: Reported questions use normal statement word order (subject + verb), without do/did, and the tense usually moves back.

grammar.prompt: If we ___ earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
grammar.explanation: Third conditional (an imaginary past): if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

grammar.prompt: Jake has been driving for ten hours without a break. He ___ be exhausted.
grammar.explanation: 'Must' expresses a logical conclusion: we are almost sure it is true.

grammar.prompt: I wish I ___ how to swim. Everyone else is having fun in the pool.
grammar.explanation: 'Wish' + past simple describes a present situation we would like to be different.

grammar.prompt: The streets are all wet. It ___ during the night.
grammar.explanation: For a logical conclusion about the past, use must have + past participle.

grammar.prompt: If I had accepted that job in London, I ___ in a much bigger city now.
grammar.explanation: Mixed conditional: an imaginary past condition (had accepted) with a present result (would live … now).

grammar.prompt: The painting ___ to be worth more than a million dollars.
grammar.explanation: Impersonal passive: subject + is believed/said/thought + to-infinitive. It means 'people believe that…'.

grammar.prompt: She passed all her exams with top marks, ___ surprised everyone.
grammar.explanation: A non-defining relative clause that refers to the whole previous idea uses ', which'. 'That' is not used after a comma.

grammar.prompt: I'd rather you ___ (not / smoke) in the house, if you don't mind.
grammar.explanation: 'Would rather' + another person + past simple expresses a preference about the present or future.

grammar.prompt: ___ all the documents twice, she finally sent off her application.
grammar.explanation: A perfect participle clause (having + past participle) shows that one action was completed before another by the same subject.

grammar.prompt: ___ I known about the traffic, I would have taken the train.
grammar.explanation: In a formal third conditional, 'if' can be dropped and the auxiliary moved forward: Had I known = If I had known.

grammar.prompt: Not until the results were published ___ how serious the problem was.
grammar.explanation: After a fronted negative expression such as 'Not until…', the main clause uses question-style inversion: did we realise.

grammar.prompt: The lawyer requested that the documents ___ to her office by Friday.
grammar.explanation: After verbs like request, insist and recommend, formal English uses the subjunctive (base form): that the documents be sent.

grammar.prompt: ___ was the demand for tickets that the website crashed within minutes.
grammar.explanation: 'Such + be + noun phrase + that…' is an emphatic inversion meaning 'The demand was so great that…'.

vocabulary.prompt: I'm really ___ — I haven't eaten anything since breakfast.
vocabulary.explanation: When you need food, you are hungry. 'Thirsty' is about drinks.

vocabulary.prompt: Could you ___ a photo of us, please?
vocabulary.explanation: The collocation is 'take a photo'.

vocabulary.prompt: The opposite of 'cheap' is…
vocabulary.explanation: Something cheap costs little money; something expensive costs a lot.

vocabulary.prompt: We ___ dinner at a nice restaurant last night.
vocabulary.explanation: We 'have' meals: have breakfast, have lunch, have dinner. You 'make' dinner when you cook it.

vocabulary.prompt: It's warm in here. Why don't you ___ your jacket?
vocabulary.explanation: 'Take off' clothes = remove them. 'Put on' is the opposite.

vocabulary.prompt: The film was so ___ that I fell asleep halfway through.
vocabulary.explanation: -ing adjectives describe the thing (a boring film); -ed adjectives describe how people feel (I was bored).

vocabulary.prompt: Excuse me, could you ___ me the way to the station?
vocabulary.explanation: 'Tell' takes a person directly: tell me the way. 'Say' and 'explain' need 'to' before the person.

vocabulary.prompt: Your English is getting better. You're ___ really good progress.
vocabulary.explanation: The collocation is 'make progress'.

vocabulary.prompt: 'The flats in this new building are quite affordable.' — 'Affordable' means…
options: cheap enough for most people to buy
vocabulary.explanation: If you can afford something, you have enough money for it. Affordable = not too expensive.

vocabulary.prompt: I'm trying to ___ smoking, but it's really hard.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Give up' = stop doing a habit. 'Take up' = start a new activity.

vocabulary.prompt: He was very ___ when he didn't get the job.
vocabulary.explanation: We need an adjective describing how he felt → disappointed.

vocabulary.prompt: I'm not very ___ on horror films — I prefer comedies.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Keen on' = like. The others take different prepositions: fond of, interested in, happy with.

vocabulary.prompt: We had to ___ the meeting until next week because the manager was ill.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Put off' = postpone, move to a later time.

vocabulary.prompt: I'd like to ___ a complaint about the service in your restaurant.
vocabulary.explanation: The collocation is 'make a complaint'.

vocabulary.prompt: It was very ___ of you to bring an umbrella — it's pouring with rain.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Sensible' = showing good judgement. 'Sensitive' = easily upset or aware of others' feelings.

vocabulary.prompt: Thank you so much for your help — I really ___ it.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Appreciate' = be grateful for something. We thank a person, not 'it'.

vocabulary.prompt: I've been feeling a bit ___ the weather all week — I've got a cold and a sore throat.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Under the weather' = slightly ill.

vocabulary.prompt: 'The instructions were so vague that nobody knew exactly what to do.' — 'Vague' means…
vocabulary.explanation: Vague = not clear, without enough detail.

vocabulary.prompt: The new law is expected to ___ major changes in the industry.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Bring about' = cause something to happen.

vocabulary.prompt: The results of the survey were ___ different from what we had expected.
vocabulary.explanation: We need an adverb to modify the adjective 'different' → significantly.

vocabulary.prompt: The government has ___ a lot of criticism for its decision to close the hospital.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Come in for criticism' = receive criticism. 'Come up with' = think of an idea; 'come down with' = catch an illness.

vocabulary.prompt: 'The minister tried to downplay the problem.' — 'Downplay' means…
options: make it seem less important than it really is
make it seem worse than it really is
vocabulary.explanation: To downplay something = to make it seem less serious or important. The opposite is 'exaggerate'.

vocabulary.prompt: The DNA evidence was ___: it proved beyond doubt that he had been at the scene.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Conclusive' = proving something, removing all doubt. 'Inconclusive' means the opposite.

vocabulary.prompt: After years of not speaking to each other, the two brothers finally decided to bury the ___.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' = end a disagreement and become friendly again.

vocabulary.prompt: 'The committee's report was scathing about the way the project had been managed.' — 'Scathing' means…
vocabulary.explanation: Scathing = severely and harshly critical.

vocabulary.prompt: The company went to great ___ to keep the news secret.
vocabulary.explanation: 'Go to great lengths' = make a very big effort to achieve something.

reading.title: Why I Swapped My Car for a Bike
text: Last spring, I made a decision that surprised my friends: I sold my car and bought a bike. I live about six kilometres from my office, and every morning I used to sit in traffic for forty minutes. I was spending a lot of money on petrol and parking, and I often arrived at work feeling stressed.

The first two weeks were hard. My legs hurt, and one day I got completely wet in a sudden storm. Now I keep a spare shirt in my desk drawer, just in case. But after a month, I started to notice some changes. I was sleeping better, I had more energy in the afternoons, and the journey took only twenty-five minutes.

Of course, cycling isn't perfect. In winter it's too cold and icy, so from December to February I take the bus. And when I need to carry heavy shopping, I borrow my brother's car. Still, I don't miss driving at all. If you live close to work, I really recommend trying it — even just once or twice a week.

extra; kept in case you need it

reading.title: Is Boredom Good for You?
text: Most of us will do almost anything to avoid being bored. We check our phones while waiting for the kettle to boil, listen to podcasts on short walks and scroll through the news in queues. Thanks to smartphones, it is now possible to go an entire day without experiencing a single dull moment. But some psychologists are beginning to ask whether this constant stimulation comes at a cost.

In one study, researchers asked a group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a phone book — a deliberately tedious task. Afterwards, this group and a second group, who had not done the boring task, were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The volunteers who had been bored came up with noticeably more creative ideas.

The explanation, the researchers suggest, is that boredom pushes the mind to search for something more interesting. When there is nothing outside us to hold our attention, we turn inwards: we daydream, make connections between unrelated ideas and imagine new possibilities. In other words, boredom may be less a waste of time than a signal that the brain is looking for something new to do.

None of this means that we should deliberately make our lives dull. Long periods of boredom, especially at work, are linked to stress and poor performance. However, the occasional empty moment may be worth protecting. The next time you are standing in a queue, you might try leaving your phone in your pocket. You may be surprised by where your thoughts take you.

a line of people waiting for something

to think about pleasant things instead of what you are doing

reading.title: Why More Roads Rarely Mean Less Traffic
text: For much of the twentieth century, the solution to traffic congestion seemed self-evident: if the roads are full, build more of them. Planners widened motorways, added lanes and constructed ring roads, confident that the extra capacity would allow traffic to flow freely. Yet in city after city, the relief proved short-lived. Within a few years, the new lanes were as clogged as the old ones had been.

Transport economists have a name for this phenomenon: induced demand. The principle is deceptively simple. When a road becomes faster to use, the cost of driving — measured not only in money but in time — falls, and people respond accordingly. Some who previously took the train switch to their cars; others make journeys they would once have avoided altogether, or move further from their workplaces, assuming the commute will be manageable. The additional capacity, in effect, generates its own traffic.

The evidence for this effect is by now substantial. One widely cited study of American cities found that the distance driven increased almost exactly in proportion to the expansion of the road network. Notably, the reverse also appears to hold. When roads are closed or narrowed, whether by design or following a disaster, the chaos that officials predict frequently fails to materialise. A proportion of the traffic simply evaporates, as drivers change their routes, their timing or their mode of transport.

None of this implies that road-building is never justified; a new bypass may genuinely divert heavy lorries away from a historic town centre. It does suggest, however, that congestion cannot be engineered away through construction alone. Increasingly, cities are turning instead to measures that manage demand rather than accommodate it: congestion charging, investment in public transport and the reallocation of street space to pedestrians and cyclists. Such policies are rarely popular at first, and the politicians who introduce them tend to face fierce opposition. Yet where they have been sustained, resistance has often softened. In Stockholm, for example, support for congestion charging grew considerably once residents could see the benefits for themselves.

listening.title: Sleep and memory
listening.context: A podcast host interviews a scientist who studies sleep and memory.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Today I'm talking to Doctor James Reid, who studies memory and sleep. James, a lot of our listeners are learning languages. Does sleep really make a difference?

lines.speaker: Dr Reid
lines.text: It makes a huge difference, and it's something people tend to overlook. When you learn new words during the day, they're only stored temporarily at first. It's largely during deep sleep that the brain replays that information and moves it into long-term memory.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: So staying up all night before an exam isn't a great idea.

lines.speaker: Dr Reid
lines.text: Honestly, it's one of the worst things you can do. You might cram in a lot of information, but without sleep, much of it simply won't stick. In one of our studies, people who slept after learning a list of words remembered significantly more of them a week later than people who stayed awake.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: So what would you recommend?

lines.speaker: Dr Reid
lines.text: Spread your learning out. Twenty minutes of review in the evening, followed by a good night's sleep, is far more effective than three hours of panic the night before. And a short nap after studying seems to help too, although we're still working out exactly why.

gist.prompt: What is the main message of the interview?
options: Sleep plays an important role in remembering what we learn.
Adults find it harder to learn languages than children.
Naps are better than a full night's sleep.
Students should study for longer every evening.

detail.prompt: According to Dr Reid, what happens during deep sleep?
options: The brain moves new information into long-term memory.
The brain deletes information it doesn't need.
People learn new words more quickly.
detail.explanation: 'The brain replays that information and moves it into long-term memory.'

detail.prompt: Dr Reid knows exactly why short naps help memory.

listening.title: The planning fallacy
listening.context: An extract from a university lecture on the psychology of decision-making.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Let's turn now to what's known as the planning fallacy. The term was coined by the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in the late nineteen-seventies, and it describes our remarkably persistent tendency to underestimate how long a task will take, even when we have plenty of experience that should tell us otherwise.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Now, what's striking here isn't simply that people are optimistic. It's that they remain optimistic about the task in front of them while readily admitting that similar tasks in the past overran. Students who'll happily tell you that every previous essay was finished at the last minute will still confidently predict that this one will be done a week early.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: So why does this happen? One compelling explanation is that when we plan, we adopt what's called an inside view. We focus on the specifics of the task and picture a scenario in which everything goes more or less to plan. What we tend to neglect is the base rate: how long projects like this one actually take, on average.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: And that points to the most effective remedy, which is, in a sense, rather humbling. Rather than building an estimate from the ground up, you start with the outside view. You find a set of comparable projects, look at how long they really took, and only then adjust for whatever is genuinely different about your case.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Interestingly, the effect is much weaker when we're estimating other people's tasks. We're quite capable of seeing that a colleague's plan is unrealistic; it's our own that we view through rose-tinted glasses.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Which is perhaps why one of the simplest practical tips is to ask someone who isn't involved in the project how long they think it'll take, and then to take their answer seriously.

gist.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: Why people underestimate how long their own tasks will take, and how to correct this
Why students always finish their essays at the last minute
The careers of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky
How to manage large engineering projects

detail.prompt: According to the lecturer, what is surprising about the planning fallacy?
options: People stay optimistic even though they know similar tasks took longer in the past.
Experienced people make worse estimates than beginners.
People are more accurate when a task is familiar to them.
detail.explanation: People remain optimistic 'while readily admitting that similar tasks in the past overran'.

detail.prompt: What does the lecturer describe as the most effective remedy?
options: Basing the estimate on how long comparable projects actually took
Planning each step of the task in more detail
Adding an extra week to every estimate
Working on several tasks at the same time
detail.explanation: The 'outside view': start from comparable projects, then adjust.
